title: Floyd

jokes.text: I met him on kdate, which is the personals section of the Kraft Foods website.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Liz about a breakfast date and who the guy is.
jokes.punchline: She met him on the personals section of the Kraft Foods website — implying she is so food-obsessed she's dating through a food company's site.
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock character-specific absurdism. The Kraft Foods detail is perfectly specific and perfectly Liz — it's not just 'a weird dating site' but a food brand's site. Strong character integration because only Liz Lemon would end up on this.

jokes.text: He owns a cockatiel named Arliss. / Oh, God.
jokes.setup: Liz describes her date from the Kraft Foods dating site.
jokes.punchline: The only detail she gives is that he owns a cockatiel named Arliss, which prompts an immediate 'Oh, God' — the name 'Arliss' doing specific comedic work as an old-man pet name.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Arliss' as the cockatiel name elevates this above a generic 'weird pet' joke. The reaction beat lands cleanly. Economy is excellent — three words do all the work.

jokes.text: Okay, universe, send me a white football player — no kickers or linemen.
jokes.setup: Liz is excited Floyd called back, attributing it to positive energy she put out into the universe.
jokes.punchline: She immediately follows up her gratitude to the universe with a new, highly specific, racially-tinged request for another man.
jokes.explanation: The joke is layered: Liz's performative spirituality collapses instantly into crude specificity, the racial qualifier is self-aware and absurd, and 'no kickers or linemen' shows she's thought about this in granular detail. The escalation from gratitude to shopping list is perfectly paced.

jokes.text: Danny was nominated for a Juno, which is like a Canadian Grammy.
jokes.setup: Pete announces Danny's nomination.
jokes.punchline: The immediate parenthetical 'which is like a Canadian Grammy' deflates any prestige the award might carry.
jokes.explanation: A reliable formula — the X is like a lesser Y — but executed cleanly. The show's anti-Canada running attitude gives it context. Functional and efficient.

jokes.text: ♪ The crowd's getting loud / Scotiabank Place / Make a hockey-loving face / At Scotiabank Place ♪
jokes.setup: Danny explains the psych-up song he recorded for the Ottawa Senators.
jokes.punchline: He actually sings it and it is hilariously terrible — repetitive, inane, with 'Scotiabank Place' as a baffling lyrical anchor and 'make a hockey-loving face' as an absurd imperative.
jokes.explanation: The commitment to making the song authentically bad is the joke — 'make a hockey-loving face' is a genuinely inspired piece of terrible songwriting. The corporate sponsor placement mid-lyric is perfectly absurd. Earns its laughs through specificity of awfulness.

jokes.text: It's an honor just to be nominated in the same category as Sir Dave Coulier.
jokes.setup: Danny is gracious about his nomination.
jokes.punchline: The honoree he name-drops is Dave Coulier (Joey from Full House), knighted as 'Sir Dave Coulier' — both deflating Canadian cultural prestige and landing a specific pop-culture joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'Sir' prefix is funny on its own; attaching it to Dave Coulier specifically is what elevates it. Canadian cultural commentary delivered with genuine precision.

jokes.text: There's gonna be a profile of me in the New York Times as filler because of dwindling ad sales.
jokes.setup: Danny is enthusiastically reporting the good news about his Times profile.
jokes.punchline: He cheerfully explains the profile is filler due to dwindling ad revenue — completely undermining the prestige while remaining obliviously positive.
jokes.explanation: Smart media commentary wrapped in character comedy — Danny's relentless positivity makes him blind to how his own news is self-deflating. The specificity of 'dwindling ad sales' gives it real-world satirical bite.

jokes.text: I am sick of that guy's positive energy.
jokes.setup: Danny has just finished being relentlessly, exhaustingly positive about everything.
jokes.punchline: Frank voices exactly what the audience is thinking in the most direct possible way.
jokes.explanation: Clean audience-surrogate joke. The setup is well-earned after Danny's unbroken optimism. A bit obvious but delivered at exactly the right beat.

jokes.text: Like, what if we trick him into kissing me? It'd be so funny because I'm not gay.
jokes.setup: The writers are brainstorming pranks to play on Danny.
jokes.punchline: Lutz's idea is to trick Danny into kissing him, with the justification that it's funny because he's not gay — the logic is circular and the prank would humiliate Lutz as much as Danny.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Lutz's self-defeating logic, and the implication that his enthusiasm for the idea is suspect. The parenthetical disclaimer 'because I'm not gay' does more comedic work than the setup.

jokes.text: This is the most friends I've ever had.
jokes.setup: The writers have enthusiastically agreed to prank Danny together.
jokes.punchline: Lutz, clearly the most pathetically isolated of the group, is moved by this moment of camaraderie.
jokes.explanation: Devastating and efficient. Five words that convey an entire tragic character backstory. Character-specific and lands with a sad-funny precision. The brevity is everything.

jokes.text: You say that so often, you should come up with a shortcut word for it, like 'ivatrennapra.'
jokes.setup: Pete tells Kenneth he has a Tracy and Jenna problem.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth suggests a portmanteau shortcut, and his suggested word is 'ivatrennapra' — an unwieldy jumble that is longer and harder to say than the original phrase.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Kenneth's shortcut is worse than the original — a perfect piece of Kenneth's well-meaning but incompetent logic. The word itself ('ivatrennapra') is phonetically funny and the show immediately uses it as a running gag.

jokes.text: Well, Danny's interview with the New York Times comes out today, so 'ivatrennapra.'
jokes.setup: Pete just learned the shortcut word 'ivatrennapra' from Kenneth.
jokes.punchline: He immediately deploys it correctly in context, landing both a callback and demonstrating he understood the concept.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the callback is the joke — it's used within seconds of being invented, rewarding attentive viewers. The structure is tight: establish, then immediately pay off.

jokes.text: A what? / If Tracy and Jenna hear about it, they'll get jealous and act out, and as much as I want to, I can't slap the brat out of them.
jokes.setup: Kenneth doesn't recognize the word Pete just used.
jokes.punchline: Pete ignores the confusion and continues his exposition, ending with the admission that he physically wants to slap Tracy and Jenna.
jokes.explanation: Pete's defeated-manager energy is always reliable. 'Slap the brat out of them' is a vivid, specific phrase that rewards Pete's character as a man at the end of his rope.

jokes.text: Yes. Tell them your stories. They'll hate that.
jokes.setup: Kenneth offers to keep Tracy and Jenna company during the plaster casting.
jokes.punchline: Pete's immediate tactical use of Kenneth's tedious storytelling as a crowd-control weapon.
jokes.explanation: Efficient and character-rich. It simultaneously comments on Kenneth's boring stories AND Pete's utilitarian approach to managing difficult talent. Economy of delivery is excellent.

jokes.text: Silly Mr. Hornberger. Always saying hate when he means love.
jokes.setup: Pete said Tracy and Jenna will hate Kenneth's stories.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's delusional reinterpretation of Pete's malice as affection — perfectly in character for his relentless positivity.
jokes.explanation: This is pure Kenneth — his worldview is so relentlessly sunny he cannot process hostility. The formal 'Mr. Hornberger' adds to the absurdity. High character integration.

jokes.text: Just tell me now if you've grown a goatee.
jokes.setup: Liz is reconnecting with Floyd on the phone and is clearly nervous.
jokes.punchline: Her most pressing concern about seeing him is whether he has a goatee — implying she considers this a dealbreaker, and also revealing her very specific aesthetic anxieties.
jokes.explanation: Specific, character-driven, and efficient. The goatee is such a particular object of dread — it's Liz Lemon's version of a red flag. 'Just tell me now' implies it's non-negotiable.

jokes.text: No, no, no goatee, just chola eyebrows.
jokes.setup: Liz asked if he grew a goatee.
jokes.punchline: He reassures her on the goatee, then drops 'just chola eyebrows' as if that's a minor clarification rather than equally alarming.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional misdirection. The setup is 'goatee yes or no,' and the answer is no — but the 'just chola eyebrows' pivot turns a reassurance into an escalation. 'Chola eyebrows' is both absurd and highly specific. The word 'just' does enormous work, treating the bizarre as incidental. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: With a female page? Don't worry. They disappear all the time.
jokes.setup: Danny says he thinks he really screwed up, and Jack assumes it's about a female page.
jokes.punchline: Jack casually notes female pages 'disappear all the time' — a deeply dark non-sequitur implying something sinister about NBC's treatment of female staff.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy — the joke is in how casually he accepts institutional wrongdoing. 'They disappear all the time' is treated as HR boilerplate. The dark implication and Jack's breezy delivery are the engine.

jokes.text: Typical liberal media. That's why I get all my news from Dick Cheney's website — dickviews.com.
jokes.setup: Danny complains about the New York Times printing things he didn't say.
jokes.punchline: Jack's reflexive anti-liberal media take, capped by the revelation he gets news from 'dickviews.com' — a Cheney tribute site with an unfortunate URL.
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates from reliable Jack political joke to the specific absurdity of 'dickviews.com' — the double entendre in the URL is the punchline. Jack's unironic delivery of it is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: I never said that Liz banged her way to the middle, or that Jenna kidnapped a Swedish au pair to use as a hair farm, and I never called Tracy clean and articulate.
jokes.setup: Danny is listing the false things printed about him in the fake Times article.
jokes.punchline: Three increasingly specific and absurd claims, culminating in 'hair farm' (which implies Jenna harvested human hair) and then pivoting to the racially loaded 'clean and articulate' applied to Tracy.
jokes.explanation: A perfect escalating list joke. Each item is funnier than the last: Liz's mediocrity joke ('the middle'), Jenna's hair vanity taken to horror-movie extremes, and then the Tracy racial joke which is sharp and subversive. The structure is textbook — save the best for last, and make it land on a beat of silence.

jokes.text: Why would I? He's not.
jokes.setup: Danny said he never called Tracy 'clean and articulate.'
jokes.punchline: After a beat, Danny clarifies he wouldn't say that because it isn't true — which is itself a commentary on Tracy.
jokes.explanation: The beat between the lines is the joke. The pause lets the audience process the racial politics of 'clean and articulate,' and then Danny's three-word deadpan kicker lands perfectly. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: It's a hoax. The New York Times doesn't have a staff writer named Seymour Nips.
jokes.setup: Danny is panicking about the fake Times article.
jokes.punchline: Jack calmly identifies it as a prank because of the fake byline 'Seymour Nips' — a juvenile body-part pun.
jokes.explanation: The name pun is juvenile by design — the show is aware this is a writers' room gag, and Jack's deadpan delivery ('the New York Times doesn't have...') elevates a cheap pun into a character beat.

jokes.text: My guess is this is the work of Frank, the black one, and... Lutz.
jokes.setup: Jack is identifying who pulled the prank.
jokes.punchline: Jack refers to Toofer only as 'the black one' — a beat that skewers Jack's casual racism and inability to remember non-white people's names.
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical joke that is entirely earned through Jack's established character. The pause ('and...') and then 'Lutz' as an afterthought is structurally elegant. High character integration.

jokes.text: You're handsome. / So are you, Jack. / I wasn't fishing, but thank you.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Danny the pranksters targeted him because he's everything they're not — including handsome.
jokes.punchline: Danny returns the compliment; Jack's 'I wasn't fishing, but thank you' reveals that he absolutely was fishing.
jokes.explanation: Jack's vanity is perfectly captured in three words: 'but thank you.' The 'I wasn't fishing' denial while obviously fishing is a classic comic structure, but the brevity and character specificity are excellent.

jokes.text: At Princeton, I was in a secret society. One time we snuck up to Dartmouth, put their mascot in a box, and sent it to Mexico City. We didn't know until the next day that it was an actual Indian. He didn't speak a word of English, like all Dartmouth men.
jokes.setup: Jack is bragging about his pranking credentials from Princeton.
jokes.punchline: The prank escalates from a college stunt to accidental international kidnapping of a Native American, with the kicker insulting Dartmouth men's intelligence.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The structure is flawless — it begins as a normal Ivy League brag, then escalates to an absurd international incident, and then the final kicker ('like all Dartmouth men') pivots the attention entirely, landing as commentary on elitist dismissiveness. The 'actual Indian' reveal is genuinely shocking and the total package is among the best in the episode. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft.

jokes.text: What's the most handsome animal? / The silver panther.
jokes.setup: Jack and Danny agree to team up on a prank and need a name for their partnership.
jokes.punchline: Jack frames the question as 'what's the most handsome animal' and they both immediately agree on 'silver panther' — a name that reveals both men's vanity.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the question's premise ('most handsome animal') and the two men's complete, unprompted agreement. It's a quick, punchy absurdist beat that perfectly characterizes both Jack and Danny as handsome men who know it.

jokes.text: Guess who called me? / The boob job recall center?
jokes.setup: Liz excitedly asks Jenna to guess who called.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's first guess is the boob job recall center — a joke at Jenna's expense that implies she's had bad plastic surgery.
jokes.explanation: The setup is a classic 'guess who' and Jenna's pivot to herself is in perfect character — she can only think about herself. 'Recall center' implies a product defect, which is both specific and cutting.

jokes.text: My ex-boyfriend, the only good boyfriend I've ever had — recovering alcoholic, he used to work in this building.
jokes.setup: Liz is enthusiastically describing Floyd to Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Her glowing description of her 'only good boyfriend' immediately includes 'recovering alcoholic' as if it's a neutral or positive trait.
jokes.explanation: Good Liz character joke — her standards are so low that 'recovering alcoholic' is just a biographical detail, not a red flag. The setup of 'best boyfriend' makes the qualifier land harder.

jokes.text: Cut to the Today show where Floyd is with his fiancée Kaitlin — the visual reveal that he's engaged and competing to get married on TV.
jokes.setup: Liz is rhapsodizing about Floyd and what their names sound like together: 'Liz and Floyd.'
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to the Today show segment introducing 'Floyd and Kaitlin' as a wedding contest couple — brutally undercutting Liz's fantasy.
jokes.explanation: Structurally superb comedic cut. The juxtaposition is everything — Liz says 'Liz and Floyd' and the show immediately answers with 'Floyd and Kaitlin.' The editing is the joke. Perfect 30 Rock construction.

jokes.text: Whahk?
jokes.setup: Liz sees Floyd on the Today show with his fiancée.
jokes.punchline: Her strangled, barely-verbal reaction — a sound that isn't even a word — perfectly captures the gut-punch of the reveal.
jokes.explanation: A single non-word that does enormous work. The sound design and Tina Fey's delivery of this specific vocalisation is a signature 30 Rock moment. It's simultaneously funny and emotionally true, which is the hardest thing to pull off in comedy.

jokes.text: An old Gus is the biggest catfish in the pond. Legend has it, the only bait that'll catch old Gus is a piece of old Gus himself. So every time they catch him, they cut off a little piece of him so they can catch him again.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been locked in a room with Tracy and Jenna to keep them occupied with his stories.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's rambling story about Old Gus the catfish contains an internal logical paradox — catching him to cut off a piece to catch him again — that nobody questions.
jokes.explanation: The Old Gus story is an absurdist gem dressed up as a folksy anecdote. The circular logic ('catch a piece of him to catch him') is funny on its own, and Kenneth's total sincerity makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Now, how did the very first person catch old Gus? / Well, that's a story for another time — / Right now.
jokes.setup: Kenneth tries to dodge explaining the logical paradox at the heart of the Old Gus story.
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately refuses the dodge: 'Right now.' — insisting on the impossible origin story.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's two-word refusal is perfect. It shows he's actually engaged with the story's paradox AND refuses Kenneth's escape hatch. The brevity ('Right now.') is exactly right. A great beat in a comedic sequence.

jokes.text: So if my grandfather hadn't gotten on the wrong train that day, he never would have met his wife's murderer.
jokes.setup: Kenneth pivots from the Old Gus story to what appears to be a heartwarming family anecdote.
jokes.punchline: The story ends not with a romantic or sentimental destination, but with his grandfather meeting his wife's future murderer.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke. The entire structure is built on the 'chance encounter changes everything' romance narrative, and the pivot to murder is perfectly timed and completely unexpected. The dark twist is made funnier by Kenneth's chipper delivery. Among the best jokes in the episode — comparable to the 8.0 craft anchor, exceeding it.

jokes.text: I wonder what Hawaii's state quarter is gonna be? / Nobody knows. But here are several hundred guesses — a pineapple, a coconut...
jokes.setup: Kenneth is telling stories to keep Tracy and Jenna trapped.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth non-sequiturs into Hawaii's state quarter, then reveals he has 'several hundred guesses' — implying he's prepared to enumerate them all.
jokes.explanation: 'Several hundred guesses' is the perfect escalation — it's not just a meandering tangent, it's a meandering tangent with an itemized list. The horror on Tracy and Jenna's faces (implied) is the bonus visual gag.

jokes.text: Lemon, could I have your weakness files on Frank, Toofer, and Lutz?
jokes.setup: Jack wants to retaliate against the writers.
jokes.punchline: The existence of 'weakness files' on every writer — which Jack has apparently compiled and Liz apparently maintains — implies a level of corporate surveillance and control that is darkly absurd.
jokes.explanation: The corporate psychopathy of maintaining 'weakness files' on employees is perfectly in character for Jack and perfectly absurd. No setup needed — the concept carries itself.

jokes.text: I thought that Nancy would leave her husband for me, and it's not going to happen. They're Boston Irish Catholic — they mate for life, like swans, like drunk... angry swans.
jokes.setup: Jack is empathizing with Liz about Floyd by sharing his own unrequited romantic situation.
jokes.punchline: The elegant simile 'like swans' is immediately undercut by 'like drunk... angry swans' — which perfectly characterizes Boston Irish Catholics through Jack's perspective.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke construction. 'They mate for life, like swans' is sincere and beautiful — then the pause before 'like drunk... angry swans' completely subverts it. The ellipsis before 'angry' suggests Jack is choosing his words carefully, which is itself funny. Highly quotable, strong character integration, excellent structure. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Vote for Floyd and Kaitlin. I love this woman. / Oh, my God. I can hear him on the plaza.
jokes.setup: Liz and Jack are having an emotional conversation about unrequited love.
jokes.punchline: Floyd's voice bleeds in from outside, literally intruding on Liz's emotional moment.
jokes.explanation: The intrusion of Floyd's today show presence into Liz's sanctuary is well-constructed. The irony of him yelling 'I love this woman' during Liz's conversation about romantic pipe dreams is pointed.

jokes.text: Hey, keep it down out there! / This isn't Liz.
jokes.setup: Liz shouts out the window at Floyd on the plaza below.
jokes.punchline: Floyd presumably doesn't recognize her voice and she responds 'This isn't Liz' — an absurd denial while clearly being the person who just yelled at him.
jokes.explanation: The immediacy of the denial is the joke. Liz's instinct, when caught, is to deny her own identity — which says everything about her relationship to Floyd and her emotional state.

jokes.text: You are not a silver panther.
jokes.setup: Jack is warning Liz not to seek revenge on Floyd.
jokes.punchline: His ultimate judgment — 'you are not a silver panther' — uses the just-established secret-society name as a mark of exclusivity she cannot achieve.
jokes.explanation: Good callback deployment. Using 'silver panther' as a genuine insult/exclusion works because the show committed to the bit. The absurdity of being excluded from a group that formed 20 minutes ago is the joke.

jokes.text: I mean, it's like, on TV, it used to be you couldn't say crap, and then they let that slide. And now we can say whatever we want — douche bag, asswipe. / Anal rot. / Exactly.
jokes.setup: Jack warns Liz about the slippery slope of revenge.
jokes.punchline: Liz uses TV censorship as her slippery slope metaphor, and Jack contributes 'anal rot' to the escalating list — then Liz validates it. The joke is that they've been sidetracked into casually saying 'anal rot' as a point of agreement.
jokes.explanation: Meta joke about TV standards that works because it's 30 Rock — a show on NBC making a joke about NBC standards. Jack's 'anal rot' contribution and Liz's immediate 'exactly' is a perfect comic beat.

jokes.text: So I'm simply gonna ask Floyd, as a friend and former intercourse companion...
jokes.setup: Liz is explaining her plan to Jack.
jokes.punchline: 'Former intercourse companion' as a clinical, antiseptic euphemism for ex-lover — delivered completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The clinical awkwardness of 'intercourse companion' is perfectly Liz. It's the kind of phrase someone says when they're trying to sound adult but end up sounding more awkward. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Mcshanley's? The place where you got food poisoning from the fish three times? / So? / So are you sure you're not planning to get Floyd sick and sabotage his chance of winning?
jokes.setup: Liz innocently proposes meeting Floyd at Mcshanley's.
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately identifies it as a venue with a documented history of fish food poisoning — implying Liz has unconsciously chosen this location for sabotage she hasn't consciously admitted to yet.
jokes.explanation: This joke plants a seed that pays off spectacularly later. Jack's immediate suspicion ('three times') implies pre-existing knowledge of Liz's history, and the setup of the food poisoning plan is both a plant and a joke. Good structural work.

jokes.text: Rejection from society is what created the X-Men.
jokes.setup: Jack says she'll never be a silver panther.
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate defense is to reframe social rejection as the origin story for the X-Men.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Liz Lemon line — a pop-culture self-justification that both reveals her nerdiness and her genuine rationalizing nature. The logic is airtight within its own absurdity.

jokes.text: So to get there, you start on old barn road. Then you take the first left, then the next left, then the next left, and then another left. That'll take you around the quarry, which is real pretty. I just wanted you to see it. That'll put you back on old barn road.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is telling more stories to keep Tracy and Jenna occupied.
jokes.punchline: His directions are an elaborate circle that leads nowhere — four lefts that loop back to the start — with the non-sequitur reason 'I just wanted you to see it.'
jokes.explanation: A geometrically perfect joke — four lefts literally bring you in a circle, and Kenneth's blithe non-sequitur 'I just wanted you to see it' reveals that the loop was intentional purely for the quarry view. It's a Kenneth story in miniature: wholesome, pointless, and secretly a trap.

jokes.text: We are getting a report from right here at Rockefeller Center that there is a toxic gas leak in the building. The type of gas is unknown, but it is triggering the building's autolocks.
jokes.setup: The writers (Pranksmen) present a fake news broadcast to trap Danny and Jack.
jokes.punchline: The absurdly vague and escalating fake news report — 'type of gas is unknown' and 'autolocks' — delivered as genuine news.
jokes.explanation: Sets up a good sequence. The immediate credulity of Tracy and Jenna makes this work as a platform for the escalating pranks to follow.

jokes.text: So much of my life have I wasted putting things on hats!
jokes.setup: The fake news report about a toxic gas leak has caused Frank to panic.
jokes.punchline: In what he thinks are his final moments, Frank's deepest regret is the time spent putting things on his many novelty hats.
jokes.explanation: Arguably the episode's funniest moment. Frank's hat obsession is a running visual gag throughout the series, and distilling a lifetime of regret into 'putting things on hats' is character comedy at its purest. The inversion of grammar ('So much of my life have I wasted') parodies dramatic deathbed speeches. Highly quotable, perfectly character-specific, emotionally resonant in the most absurd way. This is among the series' best jokes.

jokes.text: The monster cannot detect the smell of human skin. Anyone still inside should disrobe immediately.
jokes.setup: The fake gas leak has escalated to a fake Cloverfield-type monster.
jokes.punchline: The monster's specific vulnerability to human skin smell and the practical advice to disrobe takes the escalation to its logical absurd extreme.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from gas leak to Cloverfield monster is itself funny, but the specific detail about skin smell and the 'practical' disrobing advice elevates it. The prank's motivation (get the writers naked) is absurdly revealed.

jokes.text: I'm keeping my hat on. I don't care, man.
jokes.setup: Everyone is stripping due to the fake monster alert.
jokes.punchline: Frank refuses to remove his hat specifically — the one item that carries his deepest identity and regret — even when facing a monster.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback. After regretting his entire life of 'putting things on hats,' Frank's line in the sand is keeping the hat ON, even against a monster. It redeems and deepens the previous joke. The character specificity is exceptional — this scene only works with Frank.

jokes.text: Gentlemen, I wanted some of the TGS dancers to see this. Now we're even, guys. As you were, nerds.
jokes.setup: The writers have just been tricked into stripping.
jokes.punchline: Jack reveals the TGS dancers were invited to witness the humiliation — and then dismisses the writers with 'as you were, nerds,' perfectly contemptuous.
jokes.explanation: 'As you were, nerds' is a perfectly constructed dismissal — military syntax applied to the least military people. Jack's satisfaction in using public humiliation as currency is exactly on-brand.

jokes.text: Surculus et pruna. Surculus et pruna.
jokes.setup: The writers are reacting to Jack's prank — setting up the discovery of the Twig and Plums secret society.
jokes.punchline: Toofer's immediate Latin incantation identifies the Latin motto of a rival secret society — setting up the counter-prank.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Twig and Plums sequence. The comedy is mostly prospective — the Latin delivery is funny but this is largely a plant for the payoffs to come.

jokes.text: Now, I don't have a lot of experience reading stuff out loud to people, so I'm gonna do this the most normal way I can think of. Space, space, space, space, space, space, my autobiography, space, space, space, space, space, by Kenneth Ellen Parcell. Space, space, space, space, space. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is reading his autobiography to Tracy and Jenna to keep them occupied.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth reads his autobiography out loud including all the formatting — 'space, space, space' for every blank line, ending with 'thank you' as if concluding a presentation after reading only the title page.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely brilliant joke. Reading formatting marks aloud is a perfect absurdist concept, and Kenneth doing it while announcing he's going to read 'the most normal way I can think of' establishes the joke beautifully. The beat of 'Thank you' after reading only the title page is devastating. Among the episode's very best.

jokes.text: Liz, last night I had a very graphic dream about Kenneth. / What? Ugh! / I know. It's disgusting.
jokes.setup: Jenna approaches Liz with something clearly upsetting her.
jokes.punchline: The graphic dream is about Kenneth — a maximally unsexy person — and Jenna shares Liz's horrified reaction.
jokes.explanation: The Kenneth-as-unlikely-dream-object joke sets up a good running gag. Jenna's own horror at her dream is the right character beat — she's appalled by her own subconscious.

jokes.text: I had a dream that Kenneth and I got intimate in a portable jacuzzi. It was crazy. Glistening black and white skin — it looked like a close-up of a killer whale being born.
jokes.setup: Tracy reveals he also had a Kenneth dream.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's description escalates to 'glistening black and white skin' — a racial observation about the pairing — then the killer whale comparison, which is grotesque and specific.
jokes.explanation: The killer whale simile is a masterpiece of specific absurdism. Tracy's dreamscape logic — that this is worthy of a visual metaphor — and the selection of 'a close-up of a killer whale being born' as that metaphor is uniquely Tracy Jordan. Could only come from this character.

jokes.text: This one was so graphic. Kenneth and I were married and living in Indianapolis. We had kids. What kind of sick mind dreams that? It was disgusting!
jokes.setup: Jenna describes her escalating Kenneth nightmare.
jokes.punchline: The 'graphic' nightmare is a normal domestic life in Indianapolis — marriage, kids — which Jenna finds more horrifying than any actual sexual content.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The subversion is perfect: 'graphic' promises something lurid, but the horror for Jenna is suburban normalcy — marriage, kids, Indianapolis. This is Jenna's character distilled: she is more terrified of mundanity than anything sexual. Near-perfect structure and extremely high character integration.

jokes.text: Just like this amazing city that we live in.
jokes.setup: Tracy says he never wants to go to sleep because of the Kenneth dreams.
jokes.punchline: He non-sequiturs into a completely sincere NYC boosterism that has nothing to do with anything.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy Jordan non-sequitur. The transition from 'never sleep' to 'just like New York City' is completely surreal but Tracy delivers it as if it's a profound observation. Perfect economy — the joke is entirely in the non-connection.

jokes.text: Surculus et pruna is the motto of the Twig and Plums. And their motto is, 'Above all, be boring.' / Twig and Plums is a Princeton secret society, and Jack is clearly a member. So if someone says 'Twig and Plums' in front of a member, he has to find an excuse to leave the room, no matter what he's doing.
jokes.setup: Toofer has researched the secret society after finding the motto.
jokes.punchline: The society's motto is 'above all, be boring' — a perfect satirical skewering of Ivy League pretension — and there is a ritual compulsion to flee the room when the name is spoken.
jokes.explanation: The motto 'above all, be boring' is a sharp satirical observation about elite secret societies, and the compulsion mechanic sets up several excellent payoff jokes.

jokes.text: But during the period of the '90s... / Twig and Plums! / Thank you, folks. Excuse me, I have tickets to a Harry Connick Jr. Concert.
jokes.setup: Jack is mid-sentence in what seems to be a business meeting.
jokes.punchline: Toofer drops 'Twig and Plums' and Jack immediately invents an excuse (Harry Connick Jr. concert) and exits.
jokes.explanation: The payoff lands cleanly. The specificity of 'Harry Connick Jr. concert' as Jack's invented excuse is funny — it's such an Ivy League 1990s choice. The compulsion mechanic works exactly as promised.

jokes.text: Jack messed with the wrong fat losers.
jokes.setup: The writers have discovered their leverage over Jack.
jokes.punchline: Frank's triumphant declaration uses 'fat losers' as a term of self-identification — they have no illusions about themselves.
jokes.explanation: Self-aware self-deprecation from Frank. The joke is that their self-description as 'fat losers' is presented as a badge of honor in the context of defeating Jack Donaghy.

jokes.text: Twig and plums. / Excuse me, gentlemen. I have a, uh... veterinary appointment.
jokes.setup: Jack is in the middle of a business meeting with colleagues.
jokes.punchline: Another Twig and Plums deployment — this time the excuse is 'veterinary appointment,' even more absurd than the Harry Connick Jr. concert.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag execution. The escalating absurdity of the excuses (concert → veterinary appointment) is the right trajectory. The 'uh...' hesitation before 'veterinary appointment' implies Jack is improvising the excuse.

jokes.text: I could have sworn you watched the Early Show on CBS. / The Early Show? What am I, in a hospital?
jokes.setup: Floyd is embarrassed Liz saw him on the Today show.
jokes.punchline: Liz's rejoinder — 'What am I, in a hospital?' — perfectly positions The Early Show as something only watched by the ill and dying.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, fast media joke. 'What am I, in a hospital?' is compact and highly quotable. The CBS shade is specific and the delivery is perfect.

jokes.text: Believe me, if I had a time machine, I would go back and do it differently. / You want to split some mozzarella sticks? / Aagh! I didn't go back far enough.
jokes.setup: Floyd says he would use a time machine to tell Liz about Kaitlin differently.
jokes.punchline: Liz — already having asked about mozzarella sticks once earlier — immediately asks about mozzarella sticks again, causing Floyd to react as if this is his time-machine landing point failure.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. Floyd's time machine metaphor is immediately literalized by Liz's repetitive mozzarella sticks offer, and his 'I didn't go back far enough' treats it as genuine evidence of failed temporal navigation. The callback structure and the speed of execution are superb.

jokes.text: I was in a reenactment on America's Most Wanted once, playing a lady strangled on the toilet.
jokes.setup: Floyd mentions his fiancée is a yogaerobics instructor and ab model seeking work in New York.
jokes.punchline: Liz compares herself as a performer — her claim to fame is being a strangled toilet victim on America's Most Wanted.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Liz Lemon self-own. The specificity of 'strangled on the toilet' is exactly right — not just murdered, but murdered in the most undignified setting, and Liz offers it as her equivalent to 'yogaerobics instructor and ab model.' High character integration, highly quotable.

jokes.text: What would you like for dinner, Mr. Jordan — barbecue or me?
jokes.setup: Tracy is in the kitchen/dinner setting.
jokes.punchline: Jenna offers herself as a menu option — in the context of the Kenneth dreams, this lands as Jenna's unhinged response to the dream contamination affecting everyone.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist beat that sets up Tracy's horrified reaction. The joke is functional but thin — the setup is thin and the character integration is primarily reliant on context.

jokes.text: How do I know this isn't a dream? / Wait a minute. All my teeth are loose, so we're good. It's real.
jokes.setup: Tracy wakes from another Kenneth dream and fears reality.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's reality test is loose teeth — an actual dream symptom — but used as confirmation of reality is perfectly backwards logic.
jokes.explanation: Clever inversion of dream logic. Loose teeth is a classic dream symptom, so Jenna using it as a reality check is a sharp reversal. The casual delivery of 'so we're good' is perfect.

jokes.text: We have to Elm Street this. We have to go to sleep and kill Kenneth in our dreams.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna are desperate to stop having Kenneth dreams.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's solution is to use Nightmare on Elm Street logic — enter the dream and kill the dream person.
jokes.explanation: 'Elm Street this' as a verb is the joke's best moment — making a horror franchise into a problem-solving methodology is a Tracy Jordan specialty. Character integration is strong.

jokes.text: I don't know who the hell told you to say that, Rossitano, but you have no idea — / Twig and plums. / I have to go to an intervention for my... travel agent.
jokes.setup: Jack is beginning to dress down Frank (Rossitano) when Toofer deploys Twig and Plums again.
jokes.punchline: Jack mid-threat is forced to find an excuse — 'an intervention for my... travel agent' — the most elaborately implausible excuse yet, and the hesitation before 'travel agent' implies real-time invention.
jokes.explanation: The best Twig and Plums deployment because it interrupts Jack at his most menacing, and 'intervention for my... travel agent' is maximally absurd. The ellipsis of invention is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: So that's your second salmon. How are you feeling? / Like a rock star.
jokes.setup: Liz is watching Floyd eat salmon she knows contains uncooked Jack Daniel's sauce.
jokes.punchline: 'Like a rock star' — Floyd is unknowingly getting drunk and the phrase takes on an extra layer of irony.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony of Floyd not knowing he's getting drunk while Liz does creates a sustained cringe. 'Like a rock star' lands extra hard given the context.

jokes.text: It has alcohol in it? / No, no, he doesn't drink. / Oh, don't worry. The alcohol cooks down with the fish. / But what if you get the sauce on the side, and it isn't cooked with the fish? / That would explain why we have so many drunk kids here.
jokes.setup: Liz realizes the Jack glaze sauce contains alcohol and that Floyd has been getting it on the side, uncooked.
jokes.punchline: The waiter's casual admission that this explains the many drunk children in the restaurant — implying it's a known, ongoing issue they haven't addressed.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'oh no Floyd is accidentally drinking' to 'also there are many drunk children here' is a masterfully dark escalation. The waiter's matter-of-fact delivery of 'that would explain why we have so many drunk kids here' is structurally excellent — it treats a shocking revelation as a mild administrative mystery solved.

jokes.text: This is the slippery slope.
jokes.setup: Liz has accidentally gotten Floyd drunk through the salmon.
jokes.punchline: She invokes the exact phrase Jack used earlier — 'the slippery slope' — as her moment of self-awareness, calling back his warning.
jokes.explanation: Clean callback that pays off the earlier TV censorship metaphor. Not a huge laugh but structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: Squeeze in one last ride at Six Floyds Amusement Park? Well, we're closed. Sorry.
jokes.setup: A drunk Floyd accuses Liz of trying to get him drunk to sleep with him.
jokes.punchline: He refers to himself as 'Six Floyds Amusement Park' — a metaphor for his body/availability — which is both absurd and oddly specific ('six' implies previous visits).
jokes.explanation: Drunk Floyd's metaphor is inspired — 'Six Floyds' (riffing on Six Flags) is specific enough to imply Liz has been to this park many times. The 'we're closed, sorry' extends the metaphor with perfect logic.

jokes.text: One, blonde. Two, she's alive... like a deer. She runs and sniffs and jumps and stares. She's not like the badger with its glasses and its rules about weekday sex.
jokes.setup: A drunk Floyd explains why he's marrying Kaitlin instead of being with Liz.
jokes.punchline: His two-item list comparing Kaitlin (a deer) and Liz (a badger with glasses and rules about weekday sex) is simultaneously insulting and bizarrely affectionate toward Liz.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The deer/badger animal taxonomy is inspired — deer as a symbol of vibrant, instinctual energy versus the badger as a bespectacled rule-setter about WEEKDAY SEX. The specificity of 'rules about weekday sex' as a character flaw is simultaneously an insult and a perfect comic portrait of Liz Lemon. 'She runs and sniffs and jumps and stares' builds to perfect absurdist rhythm. Comparably excellent to the vasectomy anchor joke in structure and impact.

jokes.text: Those are good rules. People have work in the morning.
jokes.setup: Floyd has just called Liz a badger with rules about weekday sex.
jokes.punchline: Rather than defend herself against the insult, Liz defends the rules — implicitly confirming everything Floyd said.
jokes.explanation: The perfect callback to the deer/badger joke. Liz's defense is 'those are good rules' — which confirms her as the badger and doubles down on it. 'People have work in the morning' is both the most Liz Lemon thing she could say and the funniest possible response to being called a rule-obsessed badger. Exceptional economy — six words that perfectly characterize the protagonist. Among the episode's very best.

jokes.text: How are you still single, Liz? There's so many guys out there that want to be poisoned and yelled at.
jokes.setup: Liz has just confirmed she has rules about weekday sex.
jokes.punchline: Floyd's sarcastic bafflement at her singleness — framing 'poisoned and yelled at' as a desirable partner profile she somehow can't find takers for.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the accidental poisoning is immediate and sharp. 'Poisoned and yelled at' as a Liz Lemon dating profile is a devastating character summary. Well-structured and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Salmon for everyone... on me.
jokes.setup: A drunk Floyd is walking out of the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: He grandly orders salmon for the whole restaurant on his way out — salmon being the very vehicle of his accidental intoxication.
jokes.explanation: Good drunk Floyd exit gag. The circular callback to the salmon that poisoned him is the right note to end the dinner scene on.

jokes.text: Tracy and Jenna in their dreamscape — attempting to attack a dream-Kenneth, who is portrayed as a supernatural figure they're trying to kill Elm Street-style.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna have decided to 'Elm Street' Kenneth — kill him in their dreams.
jokes.punchline: The sequence of them actually attempting this, in their shared dreamscape, plays as both an action sequence and a comedy of the bizarre.
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the dream sequence. Without full visual context from the subtitle transcript, this is primarily an absurdist visual gag whose full impact depends on the staging.

jokes.text: Uh, controlling our dreams? We can explain, Pete. / Unbelievable. It is way too early for this, guys. I haven't even had my first cup of wine today.
jokes.setup: Pete walks in on Tracy and Jenna apparently acting out their dream battle.
jokes.punchline: Pete's complaint is that it's too early — followed by 'I haven't even had my first cup of wine today,' implying wine is his normal morning beverage.
jokes.explanation: 'My first cup of wine' is a superb Pete character moment — the normalization of morning wine drinking positions Pete as a man whose coping mechanisms are fully institutionalized. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Hello, Frank. I think you know where I am. I just happened to run into your mom at a T.J. Maxx in Queens, and we came back here for some cannoli and red wine. She's a lovely woman. I'll be leaving soon. I'm a gentleman... as is Danny.
jokes.setup: Jack sends a tape to Frank as counter-retaliation for the Twig and Plums harassment.
jokes.punchline: Jack has 'run into' Frank's mother at a T.J. Maxx in Queens — implying he orchestrated the encounter — and is now with her under ambiguous circumstances, ending with 'I'm a gentleman... as is Danny.'
jokes.explanation: Jack going nuclear on the writers by involving their mothers is characteristically over-the-top. 'T.J. Maxx in Queens' is a hilariously specific location that implies the mother's socioeconomic situation. 'I'm a gentleman... as is Danny' is a perfectly calibrated pause — it implies something was considered before being set aside. Highly effective.

jokes.text: Hey, Frank. Your mom's a hugger.
jokes.setup: Jack has already delivered his threat; Danny adds to it.
jokes.punchline: Danny's contribution is the completely innocent 'your mom's a hugger' — which, coming after Jack's ambiguous threats, could be read as either completely benign or deeply sinister.
jokes.explanation: Five words that land perfectly. The ambiguity between innocent and threatening is the joke, and the ambiguity is total — it's both. Danny's delivery as the 'handsome' man above the fray makes it even funnier. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: Don't push me, Frank. You won't enjoy the next tape. Your mom might, though. And I believe Toofer and Lutz also have mothers.
jokes.setup: Frank is presumably hesitating to comply.
jokes.punchline: Jack escalates — 'your mom might' enjoy the next tape (implying mutual enjoyment) and then extends the threat to Toofer's and Lutz's mothers.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the mothers threat is perfectly structured — 'your mom might' is the dark pivot, and 'I believe Toofer and Lutz also have mothers' is the devastating third beat. Jack's measured, almost-regretful delivery of this threat is the key.

jokes.text: Pranksmen... stand down.
jokes.setup: Frank has been beaten by Jack's mother gambit.
jokes.punchline: Frank's concession is delivered in military tactical language — 'stand down' — treating a writers' room prank war with absurd gravity.
jokes.explanation: Frank using 'stand down' as military language for a workplace prank war is funny precisely because of the gap between the language register and the situation. The pause before 'stand down' adds to the defeated gravity.

jokes.text: In this hour, spring cleaning — / Boring! Boring! Floyd, come on. / Hey, you guys wear so much makeup, you know that? / Floyd! Have you been drinking? / Shut up, kit kat!
jokes.setup: A drunk Floyd has returned to the Today show plaza and is heckling the hosts.
jokes.punchline: Floyd's drunken Today show appearance culminates in 'Shut up, kit kat!' — a baffling insult that suggests the host looks like a Kit Kat bar.
jokes.explanation: 'Shut up, kit kat!' is inspired drunk nonsense. It's specific, unexpected, and makes no discernible logical sense, which is exactly right for drunk Floyd.

jokes.text: Mm. / Ah, false alarm! Saved it. / All right.
jokes.setup: Liz is watching the chaos of drunk Floyd on the Today show and processing her guilt.
jokes.punchline: A physical beat — implied near-vomit or stumble — followed by Liz's 'false alarm! Saved it' as if she's the only witness to her own body's reaction.
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy beat. The 'saved it' framing implies Liz is performing normality to herself. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: To make it up to you, I hope that you'll accept these TGS mouse pads and a man's wallet with the Dateline logo on it.
jokes.setup: Liz is apologizing to Kaitlin for accidentally getting Floyd drunk.
jokes.punchline: Her makeshift apology gift — TGS mouse pads and a Dateline-branded men's wallet — is hilariously pathetic corporate swag.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a man's wallet with the Dateline logo on it' is perfect — it's not just swag, it's the wrong swag (a man's wallet, for a woman, branded with a news show). Liz's access to this is itself a character joke. The two items together paint a complete picture of an awkward corporate apology.

jokes.text: I hope that you'll accept these TGS mouse pads and a man's wallet with the Dateline logo on it.
jokes.setup: Liz is apologizing to Kaitlin and has brought gifts.
jokes.punchline: Her apology gifts are TGS mouse pads and a man's wallet with the Dateline logo — incredibly cheap, stolen from network supplies, and oddly gender-specific ('a man's wallet').
jokes.explanation: A perfect Liz gift. The 'man's wallet' with the Dateline logo implies she grabbed whatever corporate promotional items were lying around. Highly specific, highly character-appropriate, and escalates in absurdity ('a man's wallet' as an apology gift to a woman).

jokes.text: I'm not mad, Liz. This is a relief. I thought he'd gone off the wagon 'cause of me. / No. Even drunk, he only had really nice things to say about you and your butt.
jokes.setup: Kaitlin is relieved to hear Floyd's drinking was accidental.
jokes.punchline: Liz's reassurance includes 'and your butt' — Floyd apparently gave a specific glowing review of Kaitlin's posterior while drunk.
jokes.explanation: Clean punchline. 'And your butt' is added as an afterthought in a way that implies drunk Floyd waxed specifically eloquent about Kaitlin's butt. Efficient delivery.

jokes.text: God, I don't remember any of that. Did I fall down while I was with you? 'Cause my lower back is killing me.
jokes.setup: Floyd is piecing together his drunk evening.
jokes.punchline: Floyd's blackout evidence — lower back pain from an implied fall — is delivered as a diagnostic inquiry rather than an apology.
jokes.explanation: Functional blackout comedy beat. The investigative approach to his own body's evidence is good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: And if you go on a cruise for your honeymoon, may it be free of pirates. / Outie 5000.
jokes.setup: Liz is saying a heartfelt goodbye to Floyd.
jokes.punchline: The sincerity of the pirate-free cruise wish — an oddly specific blessing — followed by 'outie 5000' as a farewell, which is a very Liz Lemon piece of vernacular.
jokes.explanation: The pirate blessing is a genuinely sweet absurdist touch — it implies Liz has thought about cruise dangers and selected piracy as the most relevant. 'Outie 5000' as her exit phrase is perfect character vernacular.

jokes.text: And if you go on a cruise for your honeymoon, may it be free of pirates. Outie 5000.
jokes.setup: Liz is giving Floyd and Kaitlin her blessing as they leave.
jokes.punchline: Her blessing includes wishing them a pirate-free cruise — a specific and oddly contemporary concern — and she signs off with 'Outie 5000.'
jokes.explanation: The pirate cruise wish is a specific and absurd blessing — referencing Somali piracy concerns from the era. 'Outie 5000' as Liz's sign-off is a characteristically geeky farewell. Both elements are very Liz. The combination in a 'blessing' is sweet and funny.

jokes.text: Liz, look, maybe this is crazy, but I don't have any female friends because, you know, my body. And I was just wondering...
jokes.setup: Kaitlin approaches Liz after Floyd leaves.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't have any female friends because, you know, my body' — a blunt acknowledgment that being an ab model with a great body prevents female friendship.
jokes.explanation: 'You know, my body' as the reason for female social isolation is a sharp, self-aware joke about attractive women. The elliptical delivery implies she doesn't need to explain further.

jokes.text: And now I have agreed to do a reading from Corinthians at Floyd's wedding. So instead of avoiding seeing Floyd getting married... I'm in the wedding party. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Liz explains how her high-road approach has backfired.
jokes.punchline: Instead of avoiding Floyd's wedding, she has ended up IN the wedding party — the high road has led to maximum exposure to exactly what she was trying to avoid.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying comedic reversal. The defeated 'yeah' at the end is the right landing note. The high road / slippery slope theme finds its ultimate comic destination here.

jokes.text: I've had enough of both of you. Your bad behavior stops now! / Absolutely, sir. We promise. / And we are never, never taking you for granted again. In fact, we'd like to sing you a thank-you song.
jokes.setup: Pete confronts Tracy and Jenna over their bad behavior.
jokes.punchline: They immediately capitulate and offer a thank-you song — which is both out of character and implies they've prepared this.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the thank-you song payoff. The immediate capitulation is slightly out of character but sets up the musical finale.

jokes.text: Thank you, Kenneth. / Oh, I'll show you how to thank me.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna have sung Kenneth a thank-you song.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response — 'Oh, I'll show you how to thank me' — is uncharacteristically ominous and suggestive, taking on sinister dream-context given the Kenneth nightmare subplot.
jokes.explanation: The Kenneth callback is perfectly timed — after an episode of Tracy and Jenna trying to 'Elm Street' Kenneth out of their dreams, his final line is unexpectedly suggestive. The gap between his usual innocence and this line's implication is the joke. Strong structural callback.

jokes.text: Let's do this. Wake up, wake up, wake up, wake up, wake up. Wake up.
jokes.setup: Kenneth apparently has Tracy and Jenna in a situation and says 'Let's do this.'
jokes.punchline: The final sound/image of the episode is Kenneth repeatedly saying 'Wake up' — whether he's waking them up or doing something else is deliberately ambiguous.
jokes.explanation: A good dark button for the Kenneth subplot. 'Wake up' repeated is funny in context because of the dream theme — is he helping them or is this the new dream? The ambiguity is the joke. Solid episode-ender for this subplot.

tmdb_overview: Liz reevaluates her feelings for an old flame, Floyd, when he returns with big news, and Jack Donaghy teaches Danny Baker the finer points of pranks after the TGS writers play a trick on him. Jenna Maroney and Tracy Jordan see Kenneth Parcell in a disturbing new light after they spend a very long day listening to him tell stories about his childhood.
insight: 85-point absurdist sprint delivers 70 jokes in 24 minutes—peak density comedy.
